'''''Potamogeton crispus''''', the '''crisp-leaved pondweed''',<ref name="hellquist">{{cite web |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=39560 |title=''Potamogeton crispus'' |website=Jepson eFlora |editor=Jepson Flora Project |last1=Hellquist |first1=C. Barre |last2=Thorne |first2=Robert F. |last3=Haynes |first3=Robert R. |date=2012 |access-date=28 July 2022}}</ref> '''curly pondweed''',<ref name="knoke">{{cite web |url=https://biology.burke.washington.edu/herbarium/imagecollection/taxon.php?Taxon=Potamogeton%20crispus |publisher=Burke Museum, University of Washington |title=''Potamogeton crispus'' |last1=Knoke |first1=Don |last2=Giblin |first2=David |website=Burke Herbarium Image Collection |date=2022 |access-date=28 July 2022}}</ref> '''curly-leaf pondweed''' or '''curled pondweed''', is a species of [[aquatic plant]] (hydrophyte) native to [[Eurasia]] but an [[introduced species]] and often a [[noxious weed]] in [[North America]].

[[File:Potamogeton crispus.jpeg|frameless|left]]

==Description==
Curly-leaf pondweed is a [[rhizome|rhizomatous]] perennial herb producing a flattened, branching stem up to a meter long. The submerged leaves are alternately arranged.<ref name="knoke" />  The leaves are sessile, linear or oblong in shape, {{convert|25|–|95|mm|in|frac=8}} long and {{convert|5|–|12|mm|in|frac=32}} wide.<ref name="Preston"/> The leaves may be bright green, olive green or (especially later in the season) fibrous<ref name="hellquist" /> and brownish and have noticeably serrated margins, a feature that distinguishes them from other pondweeds. The leaves usually have wavy edges but this is not always apparent, especially on new growth.<ref name="Preston"/> [[Turion (botany)|Turions]] occur in leaf axils and at stem tips.

The [[inflorescence]] is a short spike of flowers emerging above the water surface. It flowers from May until October.<ref name="Rose"/> [[File:Potamogeton crispus turion.JPG|frameless|left]]The turions of the plant develop along with the fruits and [[Germination|germinate]], leaving the newly sprouted plants to [[Overwintering|overwinter]].<ref name=FNA/>

Although quite variable, ''P. crispus'' is usually a straightforward plant to identify. Hybrids with various other pondweeds are recorded, but these do not usually closely resemble ''P. crispus''.

There are described hybrids with ''[[Potamogeton trichoides]]'' (''P''. × ''bennettii'' <small>Fryer</small>), ''[[Potamogeton perfoliatus|P. perfoliatus]]'' (''P''. × ''cooperi'' <small>(Fryer) Fryer</small>), ''[[Potamogeton alpinus|P. alpinus]]'' (''P''. × ''olivaceus'' <small>Baagøe ex G.Fisch.</small>), ''[[Potamogeton lucens|P. lucens]]'' (''P''. × ''cadburyae'' <small>Dandy & G.Taylor</small>), ''[[Potamogeton praelongus|P. praelongus]]'' (''P''. × ''undulatus'' <small>Wolgf.</small>), ''P. ochreatus'' (''P''. × ''jacobsii'' <small>Z.Kaplan, Fehrer & Hellq.</small>) and ''P. friesii'' (''P''. × ''lintonii'' <small>Fryer</small>).<ref name=kwc2/>

==Distribution==
''Potamogeton crispus'' is native to a wide range of countries in Asia (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Indonesia (Sumatra), Japan, Kazakhstan, Korea, Kyrgyzstan, Laos, Mongolia, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, Thailand, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Vietnam); Africa, the Middle East, Australia, and Europe.<ref name="Guo"/> It has been introduced to the Americas<ref name="thayer">{{cite web |url=https://nas.er.usgs.gov/queries/factsheet.aspx?speciesID=1134 |title=''Potamogeton crispus'' (curly-leaf pondweed) |website=U.S. Geological Survey Nonindigenous Aquatic Species, Gainesville, FL |last1=Thayer |first1=D.D. |last2=Pfingsten |first2=I.A. |last3=Cao |first3=L. |last4=Berent |first4=L. |date=18 March 2016 |access-date=28 July 2022}}</ref> and New Zealand.<ref name="Guo"/><ref name="mikulyuk">{{cite web |last1=Mikulyuk |first1=Alison |last2=Nault |first2=Michelle |title=Potamogeton crispus (curlyleaf pondweed) |website=Invasive Species Compendium |publisher=Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/43664 |date=19 March 2020 |access-date=28 July 2022}}</ref>

==Ecology==
Curly pondweed is widespread and common across most of its native range, growing in standing and slow-flowing water including small ponds and ditches. It is strictly a lowland plant and requires fine substrates in standing or slow-flowing calcareous water. However, it is tolerant of significant [[nutrient pollution]], and this has allowed it to persist in intensively farmed areas where more sensitive pondweeds have declined. Its production of both seed and turions makes it relatively resistant to disturbance such as dredging, in contrast to some of the larger broad-leaved pondweeds, although cutting down to the sediment surface in the early growing season may inhibit turion production.<ref name="mikulyuk" />
[[File:Potamogeton crispus Dorset.JPG|frameless|left|In a silty stream in southern Britain]]

==Environmental impact==
This pondweed is considered an invasive species in much of North America. It was introduced to the [[Great Lakes]] and inland lakes within that region. The plant thrives in conditions normally less habitable to native plant species. It is also able to survive beneath the surface of frozen waterways and resume its rapid vegetative growth before other water plants can regrow.<ref name="thayer" />  It competes with native plant life and sometimes displaces it. Curly pondweed may clog waterways, inhibiting aquatic recreation, and is considered a nuisance in some areas.<ref name="thayer" /> It has also been introduced to South America and New Zealand.<ref name="Guo"/>

==Cultivation==
''Potamogeton crispus'' is sometimes cultivated as a pond plant, and generally makes a good garden plant. Since it starts to die back rather early, it is recommended to cut it back in July after it has flowered. In common with other pondweeds of this group it roots poorly from stem cuttings and is best propagated by division of the rhizomes or from [[Turion (botany)|turion]]s. As it has proved invasive in some areas, curly pondweed should not be grown outside its native range.<ref name="thayer" />
